subject: Surgical Triads
title: Hepatobiliary & GI Triads
preview: Classic gastrointestinal triads help recognize cholangitis, gastric volvulus and esophageal rupture without replacing diagnostic assessment.

sections.title: Charcot triad: acute cholangitis
points: Biliary obstruction with infection can cause upper abdominal pain, fever and jaundice.
Management involves urgent clinical assessment, antibiotics and timely biliary drainage when indicated.

sections.title: Reynolds pentad: systemic compromise
points: Charcot triad plus hypotension and altered mental status raises concern for severe cholangitis.
Severe disease may occur without all five classic findings.

sections.title: Borchardt and Mackler patterns
points: Borchardt: severe epigastric pain, retching with little or no vomit and difficulty passing a nasogastric tube suggest acute gastric volvulus.
Mackler: vomiting, chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema can occur after esophageal rupture, although the full combination is uncommon.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: Classic triads are memory aids; the absence of a complete triad does not exclude a serious diagnosis.

quickRevision: Charcot triad is fever, right-upper-quadrant pain and jaundice; the full triad is not always present in cholangitis.
Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and altered mentation to Charcot triad.
Borchardt triad and Mackler triad are important differential clues for acute gastric volvulus and esophageal rupture.

quiz.question: Charcot triad is associated with which hepatobiliary emergency?
quiz.explanation: Charcot triad—fever, right-upper-quadrant pain and jaundice—is a classic pattern for acute cholangitis, but its absence does not rule out the disease.
